title: Water system IQ, OQ and PQ to EU GMP Annex 15 | Aquemi
meta: IQ and OQ to protocols your QA approves, then PQ in three phases over 12 months (WHO TRS 1033, FDA guide), with alert levels set from your own data.
eyebrow: IQ · OQ · PQ · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · USP <1231> · WHO TRS 1033
headline: A qualified water system your inspector can follow, from the first weld to a full year of data
lead: We commission your water or pure steam system, execute installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) to protocols your quality unit approves, and run performance qualification (PQ) with you through the three phases a water system needs: two intensive phases of at least two weeks each, then routine monitoring until you hold at least 12 months of data across the seasons, as WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 and the FDA guide to high purity water systems describe. Your alert levels come out of that data, not out of a pharmacopoeia table.

secondary_cta.label: How FAT feeds IQ and OQ

blocks.h: Inspectors rarely fault the water. They fault the evidence behind it.
body: A water system can meet USP <645> and USP <643> every day and still produce an inspection finding. The usual causes are in the qualification file, not the pipework: an IQ that checked drawings nobody updated after the field welds, an OQ that never tested the coldest point of use during sanitization, a PQ started before the sanitization procedure was final, alert levels copied from the pharmacopoeia instead of derived from the system's own data, and a requalification that is either never done or repeated in full every year by habit.

Each of those is cheap to prevent and expensive to explain. So we plan qualification at detailed design, in a commissioning and qualification (C&Q) plan your quality unit approves, and we carry one set of requirement IDs from your user requirement specification (URS) through FAT, IQ, OQ and the PQ sampling plan. EU GMP Annex 15 (2015) sets the stages and who approves what; USP <1231>, the FDA Guide to Inspections of High Purity Water Systems and WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 (2021) set how a water system proves itself over time; the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5 and ASTM E2500 set how much of that you have to test twice.
Commissioning is part of it, but it is not the same thing. WHO TRS 1033, 11.2 puts it plainly: commissioning is documented, and it is not a replacement for qualification.

Your quality unit approves the protocol before execution (Annex 15, 2.6)
Installation qualification (IQ)
The system as installed complies with the approved design and the manufacturer's recommendations (Annex 15 glossary and 3.9)
As-built drawings, materials, welds, surface finish, slopes, dead legs, instruments and calibration, software version, manuals and maintenance requirements
Your quality unit
Operational qualification (OQ)
The system performs as intended throughout its operating ranges, including upper and lower limits and worst case (Annex 15, 3.11)

Sequences, alarms, interlocks, divert, sanitization at the coldest point, flow and temperature at peak draw, power-loss recovery, data integrity; for pure steam, EN 285 gas, dryness and superheat tests

Performance qualification (PQ)
The system delivers water of the required quality, reproducibly, in routine use and across the seasons
Three phases of sampling at every point of use and after each treatment step, with chemical and microbial testing, to at least 12 months in total
Your quality unit, phase by phase (Annex 15, 2.10)

blocks.h: The qualification lifecycle of a water system
blocks.caption: Design qualification (DQ) and FAT are covered under process design and FAT and SAT. Annex 15, 2.5 and 3.10 allow IQ and OQ to be combined into one protocol (IOQ) where the system's complexity allows. Each arrow is a formal release by your quality unit; Annex 15, 2.10 allows a conditional release to the next stage when open items have a documented no-significant-impact assessment.

blocks.h: OQ: the tests, and the worst case each one covers
rows: Operating sequences
Start-up, production, recirculation, standby, flush, sanitization, shutdown and restart after power loss
Functional specification; restart returns to a safe state without operator action
Alarms and interlocks
Each alarm and interlock in the functional specification, forced by real condition where safe, by simulated signal where not
Functional specification; tests at FAT leveraged where your quality unit accepts them (Annex 15, 3.6)
Conductivity divert
Divert at the setpoint on a real rise in conductivity, then return to service
Setpoint below your alert level; conductivity read without temperature compensation as USP <645> stage 1 requires
Sanitization
Full hot water or ozone cycle on the installed loop, with temperature or ozone measured at the coldest or most remote point
Every probe at or above setpoint for the hold time; ozone removed before return to service where the design requires it
Hydraulics at peak and minimum draw
All points of use open to the design peak, then minimum draw
Loop return pressure stays positive and return velocity stays at the design minimum (Annex 1, 6.11 asks that turbulent flow is monitored)
Temperature control
Hot or ambient loop held through draw changes; point-of-use coolers where fitted
Loop temperature within the specified band; cooled outlets at the temperature your process needs
Generator output
Flow, recovery and outlet conductivity and total organic carbon (TOC) on your feed water at design flow
USP <645>, USP <643> and the Ph. Eur. monograph you release to, with margin
Data integrity
User roles, audit trail entries, alarm and event records, time synchronization, backup and restore
21 CFR Part 11 and EU GMP Annex 11, to your computerized system validation procedure
Pure steam at the point of use
Non-condensable gases, dryness and superheat at each sterilizer or steam-in-place (SIP) point; condensate sampled for conductivity, TOC and bacterial endotoxins
EN 285 criteria where steam sterilizes; condensate to the WFI monograph (Annex 1, 6.17)

blocks.caption: Performance qualification phases · new water system
cols: Sampling, use of water and what the phase settles

rows.v: At least 2 weeks (WHO); the FDA guide describes 2 to 4 weeks
rows.m: Daily sampling of feed water, after each purification step, at every point of use and at the end of the loop. Sets operating ranges, sanitization and maintenance procedures, provisional alert and action levels and the test-failure procedure. Water is not used for manufacturing.

Same sampling programme, now with every standard operating procedure (SOP) in use. Shows consistent operation within the established ranges. Water may be used for manufacturing during this phase if phase 1 and ongoing phase 2 data show the required quality and your QA approves it (WHO TRS 1033, 11.3).

rows.v: Until phases 1 to 3 cover at least 12 months
rows.m: Routine sampling plan, reduced from phase 1 and 2 data. For WFI the FDA guide describes a daily sample from at least one point of use with every point tested weekly. Data trended, for example quarterly, and the system reviewed at the end. Water is in use. Validation is complete when you hold a full year of data.

blocks.note: Phase content from WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 (2021), 11.3 and the FDA Guide to Inspections of High Purity Water Systems; USP <1231> and the ISPE Good Practice Guide on C&Q of water and steam systems take the same seasonal view, and EU GMP Annex 1, 6.8 asks that seasonal variation in feed water is considered. Durations, points and frequencies are fixed in your PQ protocol. For a change to an existing system, WHO allows the phases and their length to be set by documented risk assessment.

blocks.h: Sample size and method decide whether your PQ data mean anything
blocks.body: The FDA guide prefers 100 to 300 mL for WFI microbial samples and calls volumes under 100 mL unacceptable, because an action level of 10 colony-forming units (CFU) per 100 mL cannot be seen in 1 mL. It also asks that point-of-use samples reflect how water is drawn. We write sample volume, sanitized sample valve or hose, flush time, transport time and temperature, test method, medium and incubation into the sampling plan before phase 1 starts, and agree them with your microbiology laboratory, so phase 1 results are comparable with the year that follows.

blocks.h: Alert and action levels: set from your PQ data, inside the specification
cols: What happens when it is exceeded
rows: Specification
The pharmacopoeial limits you release to: conductivity ≤ 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C (USP <645> stage 1), TOC ≤ 0.50 mg/L (USP <643>; Ph. Eur.), bacterial endotoxins < 0.25 EU/mL for WFI (USP <85>)
Water fails; batch impact assessed
USP, Ph. Eur. and your marketing authorization
Action level
Microbial: no higher than 100 CFU/mL for Purified Water (PW) and 10 CFU/100 mL for WFI, lower where your product or data justify it. Chemical: below the specification
Investigation for root cause and impact on product, corrective action; organisms identified for WFI (WHO TRS 1033, 12.9)
USP <1231>; FDA high purity water guide; Annex 1, 6.14
Alert level

From your phase 1 and 2 data as provisional levels, confirmed on the full year of PQ data, for example from a percentile or control limits of the data set. Reassessed after requalification and at periodic review
Reviewed and trended; early warning of drift before the action level
Annex 1, 6.13 and 6.14; WHO TRS 1033, 12.7 and 12.8
Adverse trend
A rule your quality unit agrees, for example a run of rising results or a shift in the mean, well inside the alert level
Reviewed with engineering; sanitization frequency or maintenance adjusted under change control
WHO TRS 1033, 12.7 and 12.9

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Do we really have to wait a year before using the water?
items.a: No. WHO TRS 1033 allows use during phase 2 when phase 1 and ongoing phase 2 data show the required quality and your QA approves it, and water is in use throughout phase 3. The year is how long it takes to complete validation, because it has to cover the seasonal changes in your feed water. Plan your first production batches against the end of phase 2, not the end of phase 3.

items.q: Can IQ and OQ be combined into one protocol?
items.a: Yes. Annex 15, 2.5 and 3.10 allow a combined installation and operational qualification (IOQ) where the system's complexity allows. On a packaged PW skid it often saves a review cycle; on a full generation, storage and pure steam system we usually keep them apart so IQ deviations do not hold up OQ testing of unaffected parts.

items.q: How much of IQ and OQ can FAT replace?
items.a: Documentation review and tests whose result transport and installation cannot change, where your quality unit accepts it (Annex 15, 3.6). We mark candidate tests in the C&Q plan and write the FAT protocol for your approval before execution. Water quality on your feed, site utilities and field-built piping are always proven on site. See FAT and SAT.

items.q: We work to ASTM E2500 verification, not IQ/OQ/PQ. Can you work that way?
items.a: Yes. The tests are much the same; what changes is the structure. Under ASTM E2500 and the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5, verification focuses on critical aspects found by risk assessment, subject matter experts carry more of the review, and your quality unit approves the acceptance and release. We write the C&Q plan in your model and keep the same traceability either way.

items.q: Who takes the PQ samples and who tests them?
items.a: Usually your operators and your laboratory, because the routine monitoring that follows is theirs too, and the method has to stay the same from phase 1 onward. We write or review the sampling plan, train your samplers, and [state whether Aquemi staff can take samples on site during phases 1 and 2, and through which laboratory].

items.q: What happens if an action level is exceeded during PQ?
items.a: It is a deviation under your procedure. We investigate with you: sampling technique, sample valve, the point's flush and use pattern, sanitization records and the trend at neighbouring points. The fix is verified with resampling, and if it changes a procedure or setpoint the phase may need to be extended. A PQ that shows an excursion found, explained and corrected is stronger evidence than one that shows none.

items.q: Why not use the pharmacopoeia limits as alert levels?
items.a: Because they tell you nothing until the water is already near failure. A loop that runs at 0.10 mg/L TOC and 2 CFU/100 mL needs warning long before 0.50 mg/L or 10 CFU/100 mL. Annex 1, 6.13 expects alert levels based on the system's qualification data. Microbial counts are rarely normally distributed, so a percentile of the PQ data often suits them better than a mean plus three standard deviations; your quality unit chooses the method.

items.q: Does pure steam need a three-phase PQ?
items.a: There is no pharmacopoeial three-phase rule for pure steam. We scope it by risk in the C&Q plan: condensate conductivity, TOC and endotoxin at each use point over an agreed period, and EN 285 non-condensable gas, dryness and superheat tests where the steam sterilizes, repeated periodically as Annex 1, 6.17 expects. See pure steam generators.

Annex 15, 4.1 and 4.2 ask for evaluation at a justified frequency, not a full repeat. Most sites review the system annually, as WHO TRS 1033, 14.1 suggests, and requalify only what a change, a trend or the review points to. Repeating a full IQ/OQ every year by habit costs downtime and proves little.

items.q: Can you qualify or requalify a system you did not build?
items.a: Yes. We start with a gap assessment of the existing qualification file and the installed system against Annex 15, Annex 1 and your current requirements, then propose a scope your quality unit can approve. Missing as-built drawings, a dead leg register or calibration history are the usual gaps. See upgrades and requalification.

cta.h: Send your URS or VMP. Get a draft C&Q plan back.
cta.body: Send your URS, the utilities section of your validation master plan and your points-of-use list. An engineer replies within [response time] with a draft C&Q plan: the IQ and OQ test list, the FAT tests we would mark for leverage, a PQ sampling plan by phase and the dates when your quality unit can expect to release water for use.
